slides.headline: 3 ADHD myths that need to die already
slides.sub: You've probably heard all three. Maybe you even believed them about yourself. Let's fix that.

slides.headline: ADHD is just a lack of discipline
It's a dopamine wiring difference, not laziness
slides.body: ADHD brains have reduced dopamine transporter activity in the prefrontal cortex — the region that drives motivation, follow-through, and impulse control. A 2019 meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies found measurable structural differences in five brain regions in people with ADHD. You can't 'discipline' your way out of a neurological difference any more than you can discipline yourself out of needing glasses.

slides.headline: If you can focus on games, you don't have ADHD
ADHD affects regulation, not total focus ability
slides.body: People with ADHD can hyperfocus on high-dopamine activities like gaming or a new obsession — that's actually part of the condition, not proof against it. The deficit isn't attention itself, it's the ability to voluntarily direct and sustain attention on demand. The kid who played Minecraft for four hours but couldn't finish one worksheet isn't faking either one.

slides.headline: You'd be fine if you just tried harder
ADHD brains are already working overtime
slides.body: Research by Dr. Russell Barkley shows ADHD is fundamentally a disorder of self-regulation — specifically the executive functions that let brains plan, initiate, and follow through. People with ADHD often expend significantly more cognitive effort to produce the same output as neurotypical peers, which is why burnout is so common. The report card that said 'doesn't apply herself' wasn't measuring effort — it was measuring a brain without adequate support.

slides.headline: You were never the problem.
slides.body: The myths were. Share this with someone who still needs to hear it — or save it for the next time someone tells you to just try harder.
slides.commentPrompt: Which of these myths have you heard the most? Drop the number below 👇

caption:
Three things people still say about ADHD — and why they're wrong.

ADHD isn't a discipline problem. It's a documented difference in how dopamine functions in the brain, confirmed by decades of neuroimaging research. The person who 'just needs to focus more' is usually already using twice the mental energy to keep up.

And the hyperfocus argument? That's one of the most common reasons people — especially women and girls — go undiagnosed for years. Being able to fixate on something interesting isn't proof you're fine. It's actually a hallmark of the condition.

slides.headline: how does your ADHD brain do friendship?
slides.sub: four types. one is painfully you. comment your letter.

slides.body:
You saw the text. You felt genuine warmth reading it. You composed three different replies in your head. That was six weeks ago.

You haven't stopped caring about this person — you just got swallowed by your own brain and surfaced in a different month.

You love hard and go quiet. People think you're pulling away. You're just lost in the current.

You have a thought, you send it. Then the follow-up thought. Then the voice memo clarifying the follow-up. Then 'lol sorry ignore me'.

When you like someone, the interest is ALL the way on. Your read receipts are basically a documentary of your nervous system.

You worry you're too much. You're not too much. Your brain found someone interesting and turned the volume up.

You said yes to brunch two weeks ago and meant it completely. Today is brunch day and getting dressed feels like climbing a mountain in wet clothes.

You've cancelled enough times that you started saying 'maybe' to protect them. Now you sound distant when you're actually just dysregulated.

The guilt after cancelling is worse than whatever was blocking you in the first place.

When you're in, you are ALL in. You showed up at 11pm with snacks when they were crying. You remembered the name of their awful coworker from a story told eight months ago.

But between those moments? You kind of disappear. Not on purpose. Life just got loud.

Your friendship is a highlight reel, not a highlight-free reel — and somehow the people who get it, really get it.

slides.headline: whichever letter you picked
slides.body:
None of these are personality flaws. They're all versions of the same thing — an ADHD brain struggling to regulate attention, transitions, and initiation, not love.

The ghost isn't cold. The overtexer isn't needy. The canceller isn't flaky. The ride-or-die isn't inconsistent.

They're all just working with a nervous system that doesn't do 'steady' on command.

caption:
your ADHD brain has a whole friendship style — and nobody warned you it would cause this much guilt.

The friend who ghosts but cried at your wedding toast. The one who sends nine texts and then disappears for a month. The person who cancelled four brunches and would also absolutely help you move a body.

None of it is because you don't care. It's because attention regulation affects everything — including how we show up for the people we love most.

slides.headline: Start the task your brain keeps refusing
slides.sub: Your brain isn't broken — it's dopamine-starved. Here's how to give it just enough fuel to actually begin. No discipline required.

slides.headline: Name the exact first action
slides.body: Don't write 'work on report.' Write 'open the document.' ADHD brains stall on vague tasks because working memory can't build a starting point from nothing — specificity bypasses that freeze. Example: instead of 'clean kitchen,' try 'put three things in the sink.'

slides.headline: Pair it with a dopamine anchor
slides.body: Before you start, attach something genuinely enjoyable — a specific playlist, a good drink, a candle you only light for work. Your brain needs a dopamine signal that says 'this moment is worth showing up for.' Example: the 'focus playlist' that only plays during deep work becomes a neural on-ramp over time.

slides.headline: Set a timer for ten minutes
slides.body: Tell your brain this is a ten-minute experiment, not a full work session. ADHD activation energy is the real barrier — starting feels catastrophically permanent, and a short timer makes it feel survivable. Example: 'I'm just going to read the brief for ten minutes' almost always leads to continuing.

slides.headline: Remove the decision in front of it
slides.body: If you have to choose what to work on first, your brain will spend all its dopamine on that decision and have nothing left for the actual task. The night before, write one sentence: 'tomorrow I start with ___.' Example: 'tomorrow I start with replying to Dr. Kim's email.'

slides.headline: Forgive the gap, then redirect
slides.body: When you've been avoiding for two hours and the shame spiral kicks in, that guilt is not motivation — it's activation energy's worst enemy. Acknowledge it without feeding it: 'I got stuck, that's ADHD, I'm starting now.' Example: close the Twitter tab, reread the one specific action you wrote in step one, and press go.

slides.headline: your toolkit
Your brain isn't lazy. It's waiting for the right signal.
slides.body: Start with one. literally just one.
slides.commentPrompt: Which step are you trying tonight? Drop it below — even typing it out makes it more likely to happen.

caption:
Your brain isn't broken — it's just waiting for a dopamine signal that never showed up.

ADHD task initiation isn't a willpower problem. The ADHD brain has a dopamine-regulation difference that makes starting feel genuinely, physically harder than it does for neurotypical brains — especially on low-interest tasks. The report card said 'doesn't apply herself.' What it didn't say was that her brain needed a different on-ramp.

These five steps work with your neurology instead of against it: specificity, dopamine pairing, time-boxing, pre-deciding, and self-compassion that actually unsticks you.

slides.headline: Why your brain makes daily life so hard
Task Switching Cost
slides.body:
Your brain doesn't just pause one task and start another — it has to fully unload and reload, and that process is slow and expensive neurologically.

You finally sat down to answer emails and someone asks you a question — now you can't find your way back to where you were.
You were almost ready to leave the house, got asked one thing, and lost the entire mental thread of leaving.
You switch tabs for five seconds and the thought you were building is just... gone.

slides.headline: Working Memory Gaps
slides.body:
Working memory is the mental sticky note that holds information while you use it — in ADHD, that note falls off the wall constantly, mid-task.

You walk into the kitchen for something specific and stand there completely blank.
You forget laundry in the machine until it smells, not because you don't care, but because 'out of sight' is genuinely 'out of mind'.
You were holding three things you needed to say, someone else spoke, and you lost all three.

slides.headline: Sensory Overload
slides.body:
The ADHD nervous system has a harder time filtering what's relevant — so everything comes in at roughly the same volume, all at once.

You can't think straight in a restaurant because the background noise isn't background to you.
A tag in your shirt takes up actual mental bandwidth during a meeting.
You get irritable in the afternoon for no obvious reason — it's because you've been white-knuckling sensory input all day and you're done.

slides.headline: Demand Avoidance
slides.body:
When a task feels like a demand — even one you chose, even one you want to do — something in your brain pulls hard in the opposite direction.

You genuinely want to text that friend back and somehow cannot make yourself do it for eleven days.
The thing on your to-do list that you care about most is the one you avoid longest.
You had every intention of starting at 2pm, 2pm arrived, and your body just didn't move.

slides.headline: Revenge Bedtime Procrastination
slides.body:
After a day of performing, masking, and managing, your brain refuses to surrender the only unstructured time it got — even at the cost of sleep.

It's 1am, you have to be up at 7, and you are watching a documentary about something you don't even care about.
You know you're tired. You know you should sleep. Something still won't let you close the laptop.
The report card said 'needs to work on self-control' — this is what that actually looked like.

slides.headline: You're not broken.
slides.body: Every trait here was explained to you as a character flaw. It wasn't. It isn't.
slides.commentPrompt: Which one hit hardest? Drop the number in the comments — we read every single one.

caption:
Your brain isn't being difficult. It's just working differently — and nobody gave you the manual.

Task switching that wipes your mental state. Working memory that drops information mid-sentence. Sensory input that never gets turned down. Avoidance that shows up hardest for the things you care about most. And staying up until 2am just to feel like the day was yours.

These aren't personality flaws. They're patterns with real neurological explanations — and most of us spent decades being told they were something else entirely.

slides.headline: a week of ADHD productivity (honest version)

slides.body:
New week, clean slate. I made a color-coded schedule, bought a new planner, and reorganized my entire desk.

The actual work? Starting tomorrow. Obviously.

Sat down to do the thing. Remembered I never replied to that email from March.

Spent 40 minutes drafting the perfect reply. Sent it. Opened a new tab. Forgot what I was supposed to do.

Hyperfocused for THREE hours straight. Genuinely impressive output.

It was a deep-dive into the history of the Chunnel. The report was due today. I did not work on the report.

Deadline is tomorrow. Panic has arrived and honestly? this is the most focused I've been all week.

My brain apparently needed the threat of consequence to locate the 'on' switch. Cool system.

Submitted it at 12:03am. It was fine. It was actually good.

I am exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix. Making a new color-coded schedule for next week.

slides.headline: it was never laziness
slides.body:
Every single one of those days involved a brain working overtime just to get started — not because you didn't care, but because executive function doesn't run on intention alone.

The cycle of delay, panic, output, and exhaustion is a symptom. It has a name. And it makes complete sense that your brain got here.

None of this is laziness. It's what happens when your executive function runs on pressure and interest instead of intention and time. The frustrating part isn't the output — it's knowing you're capable and still watching the week go sideways.

slides.headline: there's a word for that thing you do
slides.sub: the reason 'just leave earlier' has never once worked — not because you're careless, but because your brain genuinely cannot feel time passing the way other brains do

defs: The neurological inability to intuitively sense the passage of time — a core feature of ADHD in which the brain struggles to perceive duration, estimate how long tasks will take, or feel urgency until a deadline is immediate.
The phenomenon where you sit down to 'quickly check something' and resurface to find it is somehow both Tuesday and also dark outside.
slides.example: "I was absolutely, completely certain I had twenty more minutes — my body felt it, my gut said it — and then I looked up and the meeting had started nine minutes ago without me."

slides.headline: the report card that said 'doesn't manage her time'
slides.body: Every teacher said it. Every planner your parents bought was supposed to fix it. What nobody knew was that you weren't ignoring time — you literally could not feel it ticking. Time blindness isn't a discipline problem. It's a perception problem, the same way colorblindness isn't a failure to look hard enough.

slides.headline: the shower that swallowed an hour
slides.body: You got in the shower with plenty of time before work. You were thinking, just thinking, and when you stepped out the window to leave had already closed. It wasn't laziness and it wasn't zoning out on purpose — your brain had no internal clock sounding the alarm, because for the ADHD brain, there is only 'now' and 'not yet'.

slides.headline: the project you started the night before
slides.body: Not because you procrastinated on purpose. Because until the deadline was NOW — immediate, breathing down your neck, real — it didn't exist as an urgent thing in your nervous system. Time blindness means the future doesn't feel like a place you're moving toward. It feels like a rumor.

slides.headline: naming it changes it
slides.body: When you have language for an experience, it stops being a character flaw and starts being a thing you can actually work with. 'I have time blindness' opens the door to real strategies — external clocks, timers, visible countdowns — that 'I need to be less irresponsible' never could. The shame was never solving anything. The name might.

slides.headline: now you have the word
slides.body: use it. share it. save it for the next time someone says 'just leave earlier'.
slides.commentPrompt: What word would YOU add to the ADHD dictionary? Drop it in the comments — we're building this glossary together.

caption:
There's actually a neurological reason 'just set an alarm' doesn't fully fix it.

Time blindness is a core feature of ADHD — not a bad habit, not a personality trait. Research on ADHD and executive function (hi, Dr. Russell Barkley) consistently shows that ADHD brains struggle to perceive duration and feel urgency the way neurotypical brains do. There is no internal ticker. There is only now and not yet.

This is why you could genuinely, sincerely intend to leave on time and still be late. This is why the project that's 'due Friday' doesn't feel real until it's Thursday night. This is why people who love you are frustrated and you are also frustrated and everyone is tired.

Naming it doesn't make it disappear — but it does mean you can stop blaming your character and start building systems that actually account for how your brain works.

slides.headline: Rest is not something you earn.
slides.sub: You don't have to finish the list first.

slides.headline: You are allowed to just exist today.
slides.body: Not produce. Not catch up. Just be a person who breathes.

slides.headline: The undone things can wait one day.
slides.body: They were there last Sunday too. They survived.

slides.headline: Tired is not a character flaw.
slides.body: Your brain works harder than most people will ever understand.

slides.headline: You don't owe anyone a productive Sunday.
slides.body: Rest is maintenance, not reward. Your body already knows this.

slides.headline: your permission slip for this week
slides.body: You are allowed to leave the dishes until tomorrow and feel zero guilt about it.

slides.headline: see you monday
slides.body: same brain. no new you required.

caption:
Rest is not something you earn.

Somewhere along the way, we got the message that stillness has to be justified. That you can only stop when the inbox is empty, the laundry is folded, the week is officially wrapped up.

For ADHD brains especially, that finish line never really comes. So we never really stop.

This Sunday, you don't have to earn it. The rest is already yours.
